## Motivation

There is usually more than one way to look for a pathogen: swabs, water samples, a
visual check, pooled samples. Which is the better design? Sometimes the answer does not
depend on the decision at all. If one design's result can be produced from another's by
adding noise, the noisier one is a *garbling* of the other and can never be worth more,
whatever the payoffs and whatever the prior (Blackwell's theorem). When neither design
is a garbling of the other, the two are incomparable: which is better depends on the
decision. This vignette shows both cases, and the *deficiency*, a number that says how
far one design is from being able to imitate another.

## The problem

The problem is the frog pond of the vignette on experiments. Bd may be absent, present
at low prevalence, or present at high prevalence. The manager can do nothing, give
antifungal baths, or disinfect the pond. Utility is uninfected frogs minus `w` times
infected frogs. Infected but living frogs are not counted as population: at `w = 0`
they are ignored and at `w = 1` each cancels one uninfected frog.

**All numbers are illustrative**, not data and not estimates for any real test.

```{julia}
using DecisionAnalysis
using FiniteKernels: FiniteSpace, factors, cpt
include(joinpath("..", "_common.jl"))

actions = [:no_intervention, :antifungal_baths, :disinfect_pond]
states = [:absent, :low_prevalence, :high_prevalence]
uninfected = [500 300 100; 470 380 250; 350 340 320]
infected = [0 150 250; 0 60 120; 0 10 20]
prior = FiniteBelief(states, [1 // 2, 3 // 10, 1 // 5])

function bd_problem(w)
    return DecisionProblem(PayoffTable(actions, states, uninfected .- w .* infected),
                           prior; baseline=:no_intervention)
end

md_table(["w", "best action now", "its expected gain over no intervention", "EVPI"],
         [[w, first_choice(decide(bd_problem(w), MaxExpectedUtility())),
           maximum(expected_gain_over_baseline(bd_problem(w))), evpi(bd_problem(w))]
          for w in (0, 1)])
```

## Four designs

A swab test of a sample of frogs, as before:

```{julia}
swab = Experiment([19//20 2//5 1//20; 1//20 3//5 19//20];
                  signals=[:negative, :positive], states=states)
```

An environmental DNA (eDNA) test of pond water. It detects Bd at low prevalence better
than the swab does, and gives more false positives. This one is built from a
`FiniteKernel`, a conditional probability table of `FiniteKernels.jl`, written with one
row per state.

```{julia}
Θ = FiniteSpace(:bd, states)
Z = FiniteSpace(:edna, [:negative, :positive])
edna = Experiment(cpt(only(factors(Θ)), only(factors(Z)),
                      [4//5  1//5        # absent:          P(negative), P(positive)
                       1//10 9//10       # low prevalence
                       1//20 19//20]))   # high prevalence
```

A visual check for clinical signs. It says little about a low prevalence and is good at
picking out a high one.

```{julia}
visual = Experiment([19//20 9//10 3//10; 1//20 1//10 7//10];
                    signals=[:no_signs, :signs], states=states)
```

Pooled swabs. To save laboratory work the swabs are pooled before testing, which loses
information: a positive pool is reported negative one time in five and a negative pool
positive one time in ten. This is a garbling of the swab test. `garble(e, G)` passes the
signal of `e` through the noisy channel `G[z′, z] = P(new signal z′ | old signal z)`,
whose columns sum to one, and the likelihood of the result is `G * L`.

```{julia}
G = [9//10 1//5      # P(reported negative | truly negative), P(reported negative | truly positive)
     1//10 4//5]
pooled = garble(swab, G; signals=[:negative, :positive])
designs = ["swab" => swab, "eDNA" => edna, "visual" => visual, "pooled swabs" => pooled]

md_table(vcat("design", "signal", states),
         [vcat(name, z, collect(e.likelihood[i, :]))
          for (name, e) in designs for (i, z) in enumerate(signal_labels(e))]; digits=3)
```

## Is one design a garbling of another?

`is_garbling_of(e′, e)` answers whether `e′` could be produced from `e` by adding
noise. It returns the noise matrix as a witness, or `nothing` when there is none. The
question is settled by an exact linear programme.

```{julia}
is_garbling_of(pooled, swab)
```

The witness is the pooling matrix. The reverse is not possible:

```{julia}
is_garbling_of(swab, pooled) === nothing
```

For every pair of designs:

```{julia}
md_table(vcat("can be imitated from →", first.(designs)),
         [vcat(name′, [name′ == name ? "" : is_garbling_of(e′, e) !== nothing
                       for (name, e) in designs]) for (name′, e′) in designs])
```

A row reads: this design is a garbling of the designs marked yes. Only one pair is
ordered. Pooled swabs are a garbling of the swab. No other design can imitate any
other: the swab, the eDNA test and the visual check are pairwise incomparable.

## What ordering implies, and what incomparability implies

For the ordered pair the conclusion needs no payoff table: pooled swabs cannot be worth
more than the swab, for any `w`, any prior and any set of actions. For the incomparable
designs the ranking has to be computed, and it can change with the decision.

```{julia}
value = [evsi(bd_problem(w), e) for (_, e) in designs, w in (0, 1)]
md_table(["design", "EVSI at w = 0", "EVSI at w = 1"],
         [[name, value[i, 1], value[i, 2]] for (i, (name, _)) in enumerate(designs)])
```

```{julia}
png_figure(grouped_bars(["w = 0", "w = 1"], first.(designs), permutedims(value);
                        xlabel="weight on infected frogs",
                        ylabel="EVSI",
                        title="Value of four survey designs (illustrative)"))
```

At `w = 0` the eDNA test is worth more than the swab. At `w = 1` the swab is worth more
than the eDNA test. Neither design is better in general, and this is what
incomparability means in practice: the choice of survey has to be made with the
management decision in view. The pooled swabs are below the swab at both weights, as
they must be, and at `w = 0` they are worth exactly nothing.

## Combining designs

Running two tests gives a signal that is the pair of results. If the two results are
independent given the state, the likelihood of a pair is the product of the two
likelihoods. Either single test is a garbling of the pair (ignore the other result), so
the pair is worth at least as much as each.

```{julia}
pair_labels = [Symbol(a, :_and_, b) for a in signal_labels(swab)
               for b in signal_labels(visual)]
pair_likelihood = reduce(vcat,
                         [swab.likelihood[i:i, :] .* visual.likelihood[j:j, :]
                          for i in 1:2 for j in 1:2])
swab_and_visual = Experiment(pair_likelihood; signals=pair_labels, states=states)

is_garbling_of(swab, swab_and_visual) !== nothing,
is_garbling_of(visual, swab_and_visual) !== nothing
```

```{julia}
md_table(["design", "EVSI at w = 0", "EVSI at w = 1"],
         [[name, evsi(bd_problem(0), e), evsi(bd_problem(1), e)]
          for (name, e) in ["swab" => swab, "visual" => visual,
                            "swab and visual" => swab_and_visual]])
```

At `w = 0` adding the visual check to the swab roughly doubles the value. At `w = 1` it
adds nothing: the pair is worth exactly what the swab alone is worth, because the
visual result never changes the action that the swab result already leads to.

## Deficiency

`deficiency(e, e′)` measures how far `e` is from being able to imitate `e′`: the
smallest, over all noise matrices applied to `e`, of the largest total-variation
distance between the imitation and `e′` across states. It is zero exactly when `e′` is
a garbling of `e`. It is not symmetric.

```{julia}
md_table(vcat("deficiency of ↓ with respect to →", first.(designs)),
         [vcat(name, [deficiency(e, e′) for (_, e′) in designs]) for (name, e) in designs];
         digits=3)
```

The zeros off the diagonal mark the ordered pair: the swab imitates pooled swabs
exactly. The deficiency also bounds the damage of using the wrong design. For a payoff
table whose payoffs span a range `B`, acting on `e` falls short of acting on `e′` by at
most `B × deficiency(e, e′)`, for every prior.

```{julia}
function value_gap_bound(w, e, e′)
    Q = bd_problem(w).payoff.Q
    return (maximum(Q) - minimum(Q)) * deficiency(e, e′)
end

md_table(["w", "EVSI of eDNA − EVSI of swab", "bound B × δ(swab, eDNA)",
          "EVSI of swab − EVSI of eDNA", "bound B × δ(eDNA, swab)"],
         [[w, evsi(bd_problem(w), edna) - evsi(bd_problem(w), swab),
           value_gap_bound(w, swab, edna),
           evsi(bd_problem(w), swab) - evsi(bd_problem(w), edna),
           value_gap_bound(w, edna, swab)] for w in (0, 1)])
```

The bounds hold and are loose, as worst-case bounds over all priors usually are.

## What to take away

- `garble(e, G)` adds noise to an experiment. A garbling is never worth more than the
  original, for any decision and any single prior.
- `is_garbling_of(e′, e)` decides whether one design can be imitated from another and
  returns the noise matrix as a witness. It is exact for rational likelihoods.
- Most pairs of real designs are incomparable. Then the better design depends on the
  decision: here the eDNA test is worth more at `w = 0` and the swab at `w = 1`.
- A combined design is at least as good as each of its parts, and may be no better than
  one of them.
- `deficiency(e, e′)` is zero for a garbling and otherwise bounds, through the range of
  the payoffs, how much worse `e` can be than `e′`.
